## Preliminaries

**Working scope (declared as assumption, not fact).** Jonah 4:1-11 is taken as a single reading unit — the book's final chapter: Jonah's anger at Nineveh's sparing, the plant/worm/wind episode, and God's closing argument from pity, ending the whole book on a deliberately unresolved question. No internal scene-break. "Bearing on the inner being" includes: (a) Jonah's own interior, stated here more fully, directly, and repeatedly than anywhere else in the book (anger, a death-wish twice, gladness, unqualified self-justification); (b) God's own operations (patient questioning, providing, withdrawing, explicit self-testimony to compassion), placed in direct, textually-anchored comparison with Jonah's own states via shared vocabulary — this chapter is where Q12/B.11 finds its clearest material in the book; (c) Nineveh, referenced but not itself acting in this chapter, its "120,000 persons" enumerated as the object of the book's closing statement.

**Reading rule applied.** No [AMBIGUOUS]-span STEP-live resolution was needed — the base extract reports 100% meaning coverage for this range (152/152 non-particle spans). Hebrew narrative/dialogue prose.

**Corpus-continuity check.** Performed before writing. Read: `WA-jonah-1-debate.md`, `WA-jonah-2-debate.md`, `WA-jonah-3-debate.md`, all in full. Continuity: Jon 1 flagged Jonah's flight-motive as an unstated silence with a named forward-pointer to 4:2 (resolved directly below). Jon 3's EQ11 flagged Jonah's silence through his compliance/proclamation (resolved by 4:1's disclosed displeasure). Jon 3 also opened the Q12/B.11 method addition with its first anchored instance (3:8-10, "turn"); this chapter supplies the book's two clearest and most concentrated anchored instances (anger; pity).

## Per-verse debate

### Jon 4:1

> But it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was angry.

**Observation.** "It displeased [H7489A] Jonah [H3124] exceedingly [H1419A/H7451I], and he was angry [H2734]."

**Operation 1 — Jonah's displeasure and anger.**
- **Action-type:** was-displeased/became-angry.
- **Subject:** Jonah.
- **Operation:** a state — a directly stated interior reaction: displeasure and anger, doubly marked.
- **Source:** God's relenting toward Nineveh (3:10), the immediately preceding narrated event — a direct, textually adjacent linkage, though the text does not use an explicit causal conjunction here.
- **Target:** n/a directly stated (his own interior state); relationally, God's act of relenting (the trigger).

**Interrogative — questions considered.** (`WA-interpretation-questions` Q1-Q12 — every human mentioned in this verse is a presumptive candidate, per read-guidance step 2 note (f); a candidate that resolves to nothing is recorded as an explicit silence, per Part B.4, not omitted)
- Q1/Q2: Jonah — focused inner being; here, for the first time since ch. 2's prayer, his interior is stated directly and unambiguously — displeasure and anger, doubly marked. This directly answers EQ11 from the Jon 3 debate: his unstated disposition through 3:3-4 (compliance, proclamation) is now revealed, retrospectively, to have concealed genuine displeasure at the outcome he himself achieved.
- Q3: Stated, explicitly, doubly marked — not inferred.
- Q4: Source of the displeasure/anger = God's relenting (3:10) — the immediately preceding narrated event; the causal reading is strongly invited by sequence, not asserted by an explicit "because."
- Q5: Target = n/a directly stated (self-contained interior state).
- Q6: State.
- Q7: **Major linkage, resolving EQ11**: Jonah's silence through 3:3-4 is now shown to have masked genuine displeasure at the mission's success — the text withheld this until Nineveh was already spared, maximizing the contrast.
- Q8: N/A.
- Q9: Sufficient.
- Q11: was-displeased/became-angry.
- Q12: N/A directly this verse — the divine-mirroring content (Jonah's anger against God's own "slow to anger") is stated explicitly one verse later (4:2); flagged there.

**Decision.** Retain — resolves EQ11 from Jon 3, directly and explicitly.

### Jon 4:2

> And he prayed to the Lord and said, “ O Lord, is not this what I said when I was yet in my country? That is why I made haste to flee to Tarshish; for I knew that you are a gracious God and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, and relenting from disaster.

**Observation.** "He prayed [H6419] to the LORD [H3068G] and said, 'O LORD, is not this what I said [H1697H/H1961] when I was yet in my country [H0127H]? That is why I made haste [H6923] to flee [H1272/H9005] to Tarshish [H8659H]; for I knew [H3045] that you are a gracious [H2587] God [H0410G] and merciful [H7349], slow [H0750] to anger [H0639G] and abounding [H7227A] in steadfast love [H2617A], and relenting [H5162H] from disaster [H7451C].'"

**Operation 1 — Jonah's prayer of complaint.**
- **Action-type:** prayed/complained.
- **Subject:** Jonah.
- **Operation:** a movement — a prayer, but one of complaint/accusation, contrasting sharply with ch. 2's prayer of thanksgiving.
- **Source:** self.
- **Target:** the LORD.

**Operation 2 — Jonah's retrospective disclosure of his original motive.**
- **Action-type:** confessed/disclosed (his reason for fleeing).
- **Subject:** Jonah.
- **Operation:** a state — a stated, first-person disclosure: he fled because he knew God's character and anticipated exactly this outcome.
- **Source:** self — his own stated prior knowledge/anticipation.
- **Target:** n/a directly (a confession); relationally, the LORD.

**Operation 3 — Jonah's own quotation of God's character.**
- **Action-type:** quoted/confessed (God's character).
- **Subject:** the LORD, described by Jonah, echoing the traditional attribute-formula.
- **Operation:** a state — "gracious... merciful, slow to anger... abounding in steadfast love, and relenting from disaster" — a stated divine character, given in Jonah's own voice as the explicit reason for his flight.
- **Source:** self (God's own character, per Jonah's own testimony).
- **Target:** n/a directly — a description, though its content directly explains 3:10's relenting.

**Interrogative — questions considered.**
- Q1/Q2: Jonah — focused inner being; here his interior reaches its most complete, explicit, retrospective self-disclosure in the book — not just a present feeling (4:1) but a fully-articulated theological rationale reaching back to before the book's opening events.
- Q3: All three operations stated, explicitly, first person — not inferred. This verse retroactively resolves the Jon 1 debate's flagged insufficiency (Jonah's unstated motive for fleeing, named at 1:3's Decision).
- Q4: Source of Jonah's flight (per his own testimony) = his own foreknowledge of God's character — self-sourced, theological, not fear of Nineveh or personal danger. Source of God's character = God, self.
- Q5: Target = the LORD (the prayer's addressee); n/a directly for the character-description itself.
- Q6: Movement (prayer) and state (the disclosed motive; God's described character).
- Q7: **Major linkage, resolving the Jon 1 insufficiency**: 1:3's Decision explicitly flagged Jonah's motive as an unstated silence, with a named forward-pointer to Jon 4:2 — this verse is that exact resolution, confirming the corpus-continuity discipline correctly anticipated it. Also direct linkage to 3:9-10 ("relenting," H5162H, the same root) — Jonah's own complaint names the very attribute just narrated as having occurred.
- Q8: N/A.
- Q9: Sufficient — this verse fully supplies what 1:3 and 3:3-4 had left as named insufficiencies.
- Q11: prayed/complained; confessed/disclosed (motive); quoted/confessed (God's character).
- Q12: **Yes — the passage's foundational instance, and the book's clearest.** Jonah, in his own voice, names God's character as "slow to anger" in this very verse — the reader having just been told, one verse earlier (4:1), that Jonah himself "was angry" (H2734). The juxtaposition is immediate and textually explicit: Jonah's own quick anger stands directly against the divine attribute — slowness to anger — that he himself is in the very act of quoting. Recorded as the observation itself (a direct inversion, anchored by the shared "anger" vocabulary across 4:1 and 4:2); not elaborated into a general theological account of anger or divine-human likeness beyond what these two adjacent verses themselves state.

**Decision.** Retain all three operations. Flagged as the book's clearest Q12 instance (Jonah's own quick anger vs. the "slow to anger" he himself quotes) and as the direct resolution of the Jon 1 insufficiency regarding his flight-motive.

### Jon 4:6

> Now the Lord God appointed a plant and made it come up over Jonah, that it might be a shade over his head, to save him from his discomfort. So Jonah was exceedingly glad because of the plant.

**Observation.** "The LORD [H3068G] God [H0430G] appointed [H4487] a plant [H7021] and made it come up [H5927G] over Jonah [H3124], that it might be a shade [H6738] over his head [H7218A], to save [H5337] him from his discomfort [H7451C]. Jonah [H3124] was exceedingly [H1419A/H8057] glad [H8055] because of the plant [H7021]."

**Operation 1 — the LORD God's provision of the plant.**
- **Action-type:** appointed/provided.
- **Subject:** the LORD God — the combined divine name, a rare double-naming in this book, worth noting.
- **Operation:** a movement — a further, explicit act of provision, caring for Jonah's physical comfort despite his stated anger and death-wish.
- **Source:** self — the LORD's own initiative, kindness toward Jonah even amid Jonah's own grievance against that same kindness being shown to Nineveh.
- **Target:** Jonah — explicitly named as the beneficiary.

**Operation 2 — Jonah's gladness.**
- **Action-type:** rejoiced (exceedingly glad).
- **Subject:** Jonah.
- **Operation:** a state — a stated interior reaction, explicitly marked "exceedingly" — the same intensifier used of his displeasure at 4:1 — a deliberate structural echo.
- **Source:** the plant (God's provision), a direct, stated cause.
- **Target:** n/a directly (self-contained gladness); relationally, the plant/God's provision.

**Interrogative — questions considered.**
- Q1/Q2: Jonah — his gladness is stated directly, explicitly, and intensely — a sharp contrast with his anger, both marked with the same intensifying vocabulary. God — here shown extending kindness to Jonah personally, immediately after Jonah's own request to die (4:3) and the LORD's probing question (4:4).
- Q3: Both operations stated, explicitly.
- Q4: Source of the plant = God, self, explicit. Source of Jonah's gladness = the plant, direct and stated.
- Q5: Target of the provision = Jonah; target of the gladness = n/a directly, relationally the plant.
- Q6: Movement (the provision) and state (the gladness).
- Q7: **Direct structural linkage/contrast to 4:1**: "exceedingly displeased" (4:1) and "exceedingly glad" (4:6) share the same intensifying construction, applied to opposite reactions — both triggered by something entirely outside Jonah's own doing — a deliberate structural pairing exposing the disproportion in Jonah's own valuation, made explicit at 4:10-11.
- Q8: N/A.
- Q9: Sufficient.
- Q11: appointed/provided; rejoiced.
- Q12: A candidate, held open rather than asserted: God's continued kindness toward Jonah directly after his anger and death-wish could be read as itself enacting the "slow to anger... abounding in steadfast love" Jonah quoted at 4:2 — the pattern is present, but the text does not use the same shared vocabulary here (no "anger" or "turn" word applied to God's patience in this verse) the way it did at 3:8-10 or will at 4:10-11's "pity." Logged as an emergent question (below), per B.11, rather than asserted as a confirmed Q12 case.

**Decision.** Retain both operations. Flagged for the exceedingly-displeased/exceedingly-glad structural pairing with 4:1, and for a plausible-but-unanchored Q12 candidate, logged as emergent rather than asserted.

### Jon 4:10

> And the Lord said, “ You pity the plant, for which you did not labor, nor did you make it grow, which came into being in a night and perished in a night.

**Observation.** "The LORD [H3068G] said [H0559], 'You [H0859A] pity [H2347] the plant [H7021], for which you did not [H3808] labor [H5998], nor [H3808] did you make it grow [H1431], which came into being [H1961] in a night [H1121I/H3915] and perished [H0006] in a night [H1121I/H1961/H3915].'"

**Operation 1 — the LORD's naming of Jonah's pity for the plant.**
- **Action-type:** pitied (named, not commanded — the LORD identifies what Jonah already feels).
- **Subject:** Jonah (the LORD describes Jonah's own disposition).
- **Operation:** a state — pity/compassion for the plant, named by the LORD as a fact about Jonah's own interior, drawing out its logic.
- **Source:** Jonah — his own stated attachment to the plant, implied by 4:6's gladness and 4:8-9's grief at its loss, now named directly by God as "pity."

**Interrogative — questions considered.**
- Q1/Q2: Jonah — here the LORD directly names and analyses Jonah's own interior state ("you pity the plant") — one of the only instances in this corpus where God is shown directly diagnosing a human's inner disposition, in argument form, building toward a conclusion (4:11).
- Q3: Stated — the LORD names Jonah's pity directly, drawing an explicit contrast between its object (a short-lived, effortless plant) and what is about to be named in 4:11 (a great city of many souls).
- Q4: Source of Jonah's pity = his own attachment (unlabored, brief) — the LORD names it without disputing that Jonah genuinely feels it, only its proportion.
- Q5: Target = the plant, explicitly qualified by its cost (none) and duration (one night).
- Q6: State.
- Q7: **Q12, directly building the book's climactic comparison**: "pity" (H2347) is the operative word here, applied to Jonah's feeling for the plant — and the SAME word recurs in 4:11 applied to God's own feeling for Nineveh. This is the second major shared-vocabulary anchor in this chapter (after 4:1-2's "anger"), and arguably the book's single most important one.
- Q8: N/A this verse (Jonah is individuated; the plant is not a collective).
- Q9: Sufficient.
- Q11: pitied (named).
- Q12: **Yes — the book's second major anchored instance, directly setting up 4:11's climax.** "Pity" applied to Jonah (the plant) here, about to be applied to God (Nineveh) in the very next verse — recorded as the shared-word observation; the comparison itself (proportion, cost, scale) is the text's own explicit argument, not an imported elaboration.

**Decision.** Retain. Flagged as the second, climax-building Q12 anchor (pity: Jonah/plant vs. God/Nineveh, resolved at 4:11).

### Jon 4:11

> And should not I pity Nineveh, that great city, in which there are more than 120,000 persons who do not know their right hand from their left, and also much cattle?”

**Observation.** "Should not I [H0589] pity [H2347] Nineveh [H5210], that great [H1419A] city [H5892B], in which there are [H3426] more than [H7235A] 120,000 [H8147/H6240/H7239] persons [H0120G] who do not know [H3045] their right [H3225G] hand from their left [H8040G], and also much [H7227A] cattle [H0929]?"

**Operation 1 — God's own claimed pity for Nineveh.**
- **Action-type:** pitied (claimed, as a rhetorical question closing the book).
- **Subject:** God ("I").
- **Operation:** a state — God's own compassion for Nineveh, explicitly asserted as the book's final word, in direct, deliberate comparison with Jonah's pity for the plant (4:10).
- **Source:** self — God's own stated disposition.
- **Target:** Nineveh, explicitly enumerated: "that great city," "more than 120,000 persons who do not know their right hand from their left" (most naturally read as children, or as the population's general moral/spiritual immaturity — the text does not specify which, named below), "and also much cattle" — echoing 3:7-8's inclusion of animals in the fast.

**Interrogative — questions considered.**
- Q1/Q2: God — here directly states, in the book's final verse, a compassion whose object and scale are explicitly enumerated: a "great city," a population "more than 120,000" specifically described by their innocence/ignorance, and even the city's animals — the book's climactic, explicit statement of the very attribute (compassion, unearned) already quoted (4:2), enacted toward Jonah (4:6), and now finally, explicitly, extended in full scale to the city whose sparing set off the whole chapter's crisis.
- Q3: Stated directly, as a rhetorical question expecting agreement, not argued at length.
- Q4: Source of God's pity = self, explicit, unqualified — no stated external cause, unlike Jonah's pity for the plant (which the LORD had just characterized as arising from minimal, unlabored attachment).
- Q5: Target = Nineveh, explicitly enumerated in scale — the broadest, most explicitly detailed collective target anywhere in the book.
- Q6: State.
- Q7: **The book's climactic Q12 fulfillment**: this verse completes the comparison opened at 4:10 — Jonah's pity (small, unlabored, brief-lived plant) set directly against God's pity (a vast city, its many morally-unformed inhabitants, and even its animals) — the same word applied to both, the comparison of proportion made fully explicit by the text itself. This also completes the book's opening and closing brackets: 1:2's stated cause for the mission ("their evil has come up before me") is now answered, at the book's very end, not by a statement of judgment but by a statement of pity. The book itself ends here, unresolved as narrative (Jonah gives no recorded reply) — a deliberate, open-ended close.
- Q8: "That great city... 120,000 persons... much cattle" — the book's largest, most explicitly detailed collective, closing the recurring theme of Nineveh's scope (first named at 1:2, 3:2-3).
- Q9: Sufficient for what is stated; the meaning of "do not know their right hand from their left" is not specified by the text — named as an open question, not resolved by import.
- Q11: pitied (claimed, explicit, closing).
- Q12: **Yes — the book's climactic, fully-realized instance.** God's own pity for Nineveh's vast, morally-unformed population and animals directly answers, in scale and proportion, Jonah's pity for a single, unlabored, one-night plant (4:10) — the comparison the text itself constructs, explicitly, as its final word. Recorded as the passage's — and the book's — central mirroring instance; not elaborated into a general doctrine of divine compassion beyond what these two adjacent verses themselves state.

**Decision.** Retain. Flagged as the book's climactic Q12 fulfillment and as its deliberately unresolved, open-ended close — Jonah's own final reply, if any, is not recorded, a silence that closes the whole book, not just this passage.

## Passage-level linkages (Q7)

1. **Q12 — the book's clearest instance (anger).** 4:2's "slow to anger" (God's quoted attribute) stands in explicit, textually adjacent tension with 4:1's "he was angry" and 4:9's "I do well to be angry, angry enough to die" — the shared vocabulary anchors a direct inversion: Jonah embodies the opposite of the divine attribute he himself quotes, and does so unrepentantly.
2. **Q12 — the book's climactic instance (pity).** 4:10's "you pity the plant" and 4:11's "should not I pity Nineveh" share the identical verb, directly comparing Jonah's minimal, cost-free attachment to a single plant against God's compassion for a vast city and its populace — the book's explicit, final argument, stated by the text itself.
3. **4:2 directly resolves the Jon 1 debate's flagged insufficiency** (Jonah's unstated flight-motive, 1:3) — the corpus-continuity forward-pointer named there is now fulfilled.
4. **4:1 directly resolves EQ11 from the Jon 3 debate** (Jonah's silence through his compliance and proclamation) — his displeasure at the very success of his own mission is now disclosed.
5. **4:3 and 4:8 both repeat the identical death-wish** ("it is better for me to die than to live") but from different stated causes — theological grief (4:2-3) and physical distress (4:6-8) — an open question about whether these are one grievance or two, not resolved.
6. **4:3's death-wish contrasts with 1:12's** — there, self-sacrificial (for the sailors' sake); here, self-pitying (over Nineveh's sparing and, later, a plant) — the same request, opposite moral register.
7. **4:4's unanswered question is directly answered at 4:9** — the intervening plant/worm/wind episode is the narrative space in which Jonah's answer is prepared, not merely delayed.
8. **"Exceedingly displeased" (4:1) and "exceedingly glad" (4:6)** share the same intensifying construction, applied to opposite reactions, both triggered by events outside Jonah's own doing — a deliberate structural pairing exposing the disproportion in Jonah's own valuation, made explicit at 4:10-11.
9. The book's opening cause (1:2, "their evil has come up before me") and its closing statement (4:11, God's pity for the same city) bracket the whole book — judgment-cause to compassion-conclusion.

## Insufficiencies register

- Whether Jonah's grievance by 4:8-9 has narrowed to his own comfort (the plant) or remains primarily about Nineveh's sparing, or both entangled, is not resolved by the text.
- The meaning of "do not know their right hand from their left" (4:11) — children specifically, or the population's general moral incapacity — is not specified.
- Jonah's own reply (if any) to God's final question (4:11) is not recorded — the book ends without it.
- Whether 4:6's divine kindness to Jonah (the plant) is itself meant as a further, unstated instance of the "slow to anger... abounding in steadfast love" Jonah quoted at 4:2 is plausible but not textually confirmed by shared vocabulary in that specific verse — named as an open/emergent question, not asserted.
